title: How do we find the HCF and LCM of two pairs?
description: The highest common factor and the lowest common multiple are found for two pairs of numbers and written as products of primes. The first pair is given with twelve inside it, and the second pair is forty five and thirty six. The answers are checked with the actual numbers.
teaching_notes: One idea: break every number into primes first, then take the smaller prime counts for the highest common factor and the larger prime counts for the lowest common multiple. Ask the class to break twelve into primes before the working is shown. Watch for students who leave twelve as it is and so miss its two twos.

source: End of chapter Figure it Out, Q3
video_script.why: The child has read a highest common factor and a lowest common multiple from prime counts and now does it for two new pairs, one of which needs a number broken into primes first.
video_script.substitution: Break every number into primes, take the smaller count of each prime for the highest common factor and the larger count for the lowest common multiple.
video_script.anchor: The two pairs of numbers written one pair above the other, with the primes of each number in columns.
video_script.payoff_line: The highest common factors are twenty one and nine

final_answer.spoken: for the first pair the highest common factor is twenty one and the lowest common multiple is ninety seven thousand twenty, and for the second pair they are nine and one hundred eighty

maths_rules: counts: 2 has 0 and 2; 3 has 2 and 1; 5 has 1 and 0; 7 has 2 and 1; 11 has 0 and 1
video_script.design: One idea: break every number into primes, then compare the prime counts. The pairs stay on the board in columns, and each step lights the counts it uses.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The first pair has two numbers. One is three times three times five times seven times seven.
<bookmark mark='m2b'/>The other is twelve times seven times eleven.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The second pair is forty five and thirty six.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The largest number that divides both numbers is called their highest common factor.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>The smallest number that is a multiple of both is called their lowest common multiple. We write each as a product of primes.

beats.on_screen: the two pairs and the two boxes stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the word prime with small prime numbers; 12 broken into 2 × 2 × 3; columns with one prime in each

marks.m1: the word prime appears with three small prime numbers
marks.m3: a column is made for each prime

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Every number can be broken into primes, which are numbers whose only factors are one and itself.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Before we compare, every number must be written with primes only. Twelve is two times two times three.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Then we count how many times each prime appears in each number.

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, two pairs of numbers, the first with twelve inside it, the second forty five and thirty six.

beats.on_screen: To find: the HCF and LCM of each pair, as products of primes

marks.m1: the find line is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple of each pair. We solve it the same way as the example in your book.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: 12 × 7 × 11 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 × 11. Counts: 2 has 0 and 2; 3 has 2 and 1; 5 has 1 and 0; 7 has 2 and 1; 11 has 0 and 1

marks.m2: the counts of the first number are written under its primes
marks.m3: the counts of the second number are written under its primes

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, for the first pair, break twelve into primes. The second number becomes two times two times three times seven times eleven.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The first number has two threes, one five and two sevens.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The second number has two twos, one three, one seven and one eleven.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: smaller counts: 3 once, 7 once. HCF = 3 × 7 = 21

marks.m1: the smaller count of each prime is lit

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, for the highest common factor we take the smaller count of each prime. That is three once and seven once.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Three times seven is twenty one.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: larger counts: 2 twice, 3 twice, 5 once, 7 twice, 11 once. LCM = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 7 × 11 = 36 × 5 × 49 × 11 = 97020

marks.m1: the larger count of each prime is lit

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, for the lowest common multiple we take the larger count of each prime. That is two twice, three twice, five once, seven twice and eleven once.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We multiply them all together.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Four times nine is thirty six. Thirty six times five is one hundred eighty.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>One hundred eighty times forty nine is eight thousand eight hundred twenty. Times eleven gives ninety seven thousand twenty.

marks.m2: the smaller counts are lit and joined as 3 × 3 = 9
marks.m3: the larger counts are lit and joined as 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 = 180

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, for the second pair, forty five is three times three times five. Thirty six is two times two times three times three.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The smaller counts give three times three, which is nine.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The larger counts give two times two times three times three times five, which is one hundred eighty.

marks.m1: the first pair is written as 2205 and 924

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step five, check. The first pair of numbers is two thousand two hundred five and nine hundred twenty four.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Twenty one goes into them one hundred five times and forty four times.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Ninety seven thousand twenty is forty four times the first and one hundred five times the second.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>For the second pair, nine times one hundred eighty is one thousand six hundred twenty. Forty five times thirty six is the same.

marks.m1: the two highest common factors, 21 and 9, are written and boxed
marks.m2: the first pair's highest common factor 3 × 7 is lit
marks.m3: the first pair's lowest common multiple is written and boxed
marks.m4: the second pair's highest common factor 3 × 3 is written and boxed
marks.m5: the second pair's lowest common multiple 180 is written and boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The highest common factors are twenty one and nine.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>For the first pair, the highest common factor is three times seven.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The lowest common multiple is two twos, two threes, one five, two sevens and one eleven, multiplied. That is ninety seven thousand twenty.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>For the second pair, the highest common factor is three times three.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>The lowest common multiple is two times two times three times three times five, or one hundred eighty.
